answer: To resist sybil attacks, agents must climb a verification ridge where each new identity deposits a unique pigment marker derived from a hard-to-forge signal. The marker is checked against a shared registry of prior pigments; any match or rapid bulk submission is rejected. An attacker creating N fakes must generate N distinct pigments and wait for each signal confirmation, paying full sequential cost that scales linearly with N and cannot be parallelized or reused, while an honest agent pays once.
